title: At every ceremony
hookLine: births, weddings, deaths and every service end with the six pauris and Ardas

lines: THESE ENDINGS ARE CHOSEN, EVERY TIME.
cards: Notice how things end. A phone call trails off: okay, so, yeah, anyway, bye. A meeting ends when someone has to be somewhere else.
A party ends when the last guest finds their coat. Plenty of endings just happen.
In a Sikh community, the big days of a life end in a way that's been decided in advance, and it's the same way every time, whether the day was a wedding or a funeral.

teach.h: A WEDDING: LAAVAN, THEN THE SIX PAURIS.
teach.b: Go to a Sikh wedding. The couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib four times while the four laavan are sung. Then the sangat sings six pauris of the Anand, the first five and the fortieth, and everyone stands for Ardas.
The ceremony itself is called Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss, and in 1909 the British government in India passed an Anand Marriage Act recognizing it.

teach.h: A NAMING, A SUNDAY: THE SAME ENDING.
teach.b: Go to a naming. The Guru Granth Sahib is opened, a name is chosen from the first letter of the hymn it opens to, and again, the six pauris and Ardas. Go to an ordinary Sunday program, with an hour of kirtan and a talk.
It ends the same way. And go, if you ever have to, to the bhog that closes the reading of the Guru Granth Sahib after someone has died. The six pauris are there too.

teach.h: EVEN AFTER A DEATH, THE ANAND.
teach.b: Tradition says Guru Amar Das composed the Anand around the birth of a grandson, who was named Anand. So it began at a birth, and now it's sung at deaths too. That's the striking part.
Singing a song of bliss at a funeral isn't pretending nothing hurts.
Sikh teaching speaks of hukam, the order of the One, and Sikhs who sing the six pauris at a death speak of it as accepting that order with trust, even through tears.

teach.h: JOY OR GRIEF, HANDED BACK THE SAME WAY.
teach.b: Whatever the day held, joy or grief, it's handed back the same way: bliss sung together, and then Ardas, standing.

how: Sikh services and ceremonies, including the Anand Karaj wedding, the naming of a child and the bhog after a death, close with six pauris of the Anand, Ardas said standing, and the sharing of karah prashad.

games.q: a family gathers for the bhog after a beloved grandmother has died. how does the ceremony end?
o: with six pauris of the Anand, then Ardas.
with a eulogy and nothing more.
games.why: the same way a wedding does: the song of bliss, then Ardas, standing. Sikhs speak of it as accepting hukam with trust.

practice: Think back over yesterday's endings: your conversations, your meals, the last thing before sleep. Without judging any of it, notice whether each ending happened to you or was chosen.
Then picture one ending still ahead of you and how you'd like it to close, a thank you, a breath, a moment of quiet; if you pray, say Waheguru once.
